Night-time or waking up in the dark

constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is not very coherent for a captivity presentation as written: time-of-day could fit, but 'feeling happy or relaxed' and especially 'talks or photos about snakes' imply very different trigger themes without any supporting memory or appraisal content linking them to the captivity trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: Threat items mainly describe interpersonal pursuit/external danger (hypervigilance, checking if someone is following me, unsafe at night). That could fit captivity, but it is not well matched to the selected snake-related trigger or to body-monitoring for injury, producing a fragmented threat picture.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is much more severe and somewhat qualitatively different from the other negative appraisal items, which focus on helplessness and being unable to cope with trauma thoughts. It may occur in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Constantly check body for signs of danger or injury' fits health/injury threat, but the threat items emphasize pursuit and ambush, while the triggers emphasize time-of-day, relaxation, and snakes. This coping strategy is therefore poorly linked to the rest of the formulation and symptom pattern.

vignette:
Imran Khan, a 64-year-old warehouse worker, presents as a man hollowed out by fear. For the past eighteen months, since a business trip to his family's home region went horribly wrong, he has felt like a prisoner in his own life. The ordeal itself is a memory he fights to keep buried, a fragmented horror of being dragged from his hotel room late one evening. He was held for five days in what he remembers as a damp, earthen pit, a place of total darkness. The worst part was not the hunger or the threats from the men above, but the thing they had thrown in with him on the second day. He never saw it clearly, but he felt it: the dry, slithering weight of a snake moving against his leg in the pitch black. He spent the next three days pressed into a corner, rigid with terror, listening to its movements, certain that at any moment it would strike.

Since his release and return home, the world has become a landscape of hidden threats. The warehouse where he has worked for two decades, once a place of familiar routine, is now a source of constant alarm. The sudden roar of a forklift, the clang of a dropped pallet, or the sight of a coworker walking up behind him in the aisles sends a jolt of panic through his body. He finds himself whipping his head around constantly, checking over his shoulder for a pursuer who is never there. He has come to believe that he is fundamentally unsafe, that a terrible event is always just moments from unfolding, and that there is nothing he can do to stop it. This sense of profound helplessness has settled deep in his bones.

His home, once a sanctuary, offers little relief, especially after sundown. As evening approaches, a familiar dread begins to build. Night-time is the enemy. He cannot tolerate being in a dark room, the blackness pressing in on him, alive with the memory of the pit. Sleep has become something to be evaded at all costs. Most nights, Imran stays in the living room with the lights and television on until he collapses from sheer exhaustion on the couch, desperate to avoid the vulnerability of lying in his own bed in the dark. His wife, Fatima, finds him there in the mornings, his sleep shallow and restless. He often wakes her in the middle of the night, his heart pounding, asking her to check his pulse or feel his forehead. He is constantly scanning his own body for signs of injury or collapse, mistaking the physical symptoms of anxiety for proof of imminent death. He will ask her again and again, "Am I okay? Tell me I'm okay," needing her words to quiet the storm inside him, though the relief they provide is always fleeting.

The triggers are everywhere. He can no longer watch nature documentaries or even flip through magazines for fear of seeing a picture of a snake. When his grandson tried to show him a video on his tablet, Imran flinched back so violently he knocked the device from the boy's hands, an act that left him consumed with shame. The time on the clock turning past 11 PM can bring on a wave of nausea and cold sweat, returning him to the moment his hotel room door was kicked in. He has learned to meticulously avoid these reminders, but the effort is draining. He feels that if he were to allow himself to truly think about what happened, to let the full memory surface, he would not be able to handle it; the thought itself feels like a threat to his sanity. This constant vigilance and avoidance has left him isolated and depleted. The joy has leached out of his life, replaced by a grey, persistent exhaustion. In his darkest moments, he has begun to wonder if a life lived this way is worth living at all. It was this thought, whispered aloud one night to Fatima, that finally brought him to therapy. He is terrified of revisiting the past but is now even more afraid of his future.
